rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iram is an explanatory apposition to ʿĀd, identifying them as the first ʿĀd; it may instead be parsed as an appositive substitute.
rows.anchor: إرم عطف بيان لعلاد للأيذان بأنهم عاد الأولى تجوز أن يكون بدلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iram is indeclinable when treated as a feminine tribal name; ʿĀd is declined when treated as a people, though it too can be indeclinable as a tribe.
rows.anchor: ومنع من الصرف للعلمية والتأنيث باعتبار القبيلة وصرف عاد باعتبار الحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some supply an omitted word, taking Iram as the name of the tribe's mother; others insist it is the name of its ancestor, a view that leaves the declension unexplained.
rows.anchor: قدر بعضهم مضافا في الكلام أي سبط إرم وجعل إرم عليه اسم أمهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid, Qatada, and Ibn Ishaq take Iram as the name of the tribe, so no omitted word is needed.
rows.anchor: وبكونه اسم القبيلة قال مجاهد وقتادة وابن إسحق ولا حاجة معه إلى تقدير مضاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Pillared” describes their tall physiques by comparing their stature to columns; Ibn Abbas and Mujahid report this interpretation.
rows.anchor: والمراد ذات القدود الطوال على تشبيه قاماتهم بالأعمدة ومنه قولهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid are reported to say that the tall among them reached twelve cubits.
rows.anchor: وروي هذا عن ابن عباس ومجاهد واشتهر أنه كان قد أحدهم اثني عشر ذراعا

rows.speaker: الكواشي
rows.claim: Al-Kawashi reports that their tallest man was four hundred cubits and that one man could overturn a huge rock onto a settlement and destroy it.
rows.anchor: وفي تفسير الكواشي قالوا كان طول الطويل منهم أربعمائة ذراع وكان أحدهم يأخذ الصخرة العظيمة

rows.speaker: قتادة وابن عباس
rows.claim: Qatada and Ibn Abbas, in a report through Ata, interpret the pillars as tent poles; the people moved with their tents in spring and returned home when vegetation dried.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة وابن عباس في رواية عطاء المراد ذات الخيام والأعمدة وكانوا سيارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other commentators describe them as nomads who lived in tents and poles, moving between settled encampments and travel.
rows.anchor: وقال غير واحد كانوا بدويين أهل عمد وخيام يسكنونها حلا وارتحالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other figurative interpretations make the phrase signify elevation, dignity, firmness, or long life.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد ذات الرفعة أو ذات الوقار أو ذات الثبات وطول العمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative clause further describes Iram: no people like them in bodily size and strength had been created in the lands.
rows.anchor: صفة أخرى لها أي لم يخلق مثلهم في عظم الأجرام والقوة في بلاد الدنيا

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A raised prophetic report from al-Miqdam ibn Maʿdikarib repeats the account of their great stature; al-Alusi states no grading here.
rows.anchor: جاء في حديث مرفوع أخرجه ابن أبي حاتم وابن مردويه عن المقدام بن معد يكرب

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: One view makes Iram the name of a city, identified by Muhammad ibn Kaʿb as Alexandria.
rows.anchor: وقيل إرم اسم مدينة لهم قال محمد بن كعب هي الأسكندرية

rows.speaker: ابن المسيب والمقبري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Musayyab and al-Maqburi identify the city as Damascus.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن المسيب والمقبري هي دمشق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes Iram as the land of the people, in Oman and Hadramawt, a region of dunes and sandy expanses.
rows.anchor: وقيل اسم أرضهم وهي عمان وحضرموت وهي أرض رمال وأحقاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The identification of Alexandria or Damascus is challenged because these cities are not in the sandy al-Ahqaf; one could instead distinguish the first and later ʿĀd and their homelands.
rows.anchor: وبهذا اعترض القول بأن مدينتهم السكندرية والقول بأنها دمشق حيث أنهما ليستا من بلاد الأحقاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Iram is a city or land, an omitted “people of” is understood to preserve the grammatical attachment; the alternative ellipsis is judged awkward.
rows.anchor: وعلى القول بكونه اسم مدينتهم أو اسم أرضهم فهو بتقدير مضاف لتصحيح التبعية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators say Iram is a great city in Yemen; its descriptors refer to lofty construction and unmatched breadth, beauty, houses, and gardens.
rows.anchor: والأكثرون على أنها اسم مدينة عظيمة في أرض اليمن والوصفان لها والمراد ذات البناء الرفيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A story says Shaddad, son of ʿAd, built a paradise-like city called Iram in the desert near Aden over three hundred years, lived nine hundred years, and set out there with his subjects.
rows.anchor: ويروى أنه كان لعان ابنان شداد وشديد فملكا وقهرا ثم مات شديد وخلص الأمر لشداد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the story, a heavenly cry destroys Shaddad and his people when they are a day's journey from the completed city; al-Alusi says the story is extremely weak and fabricated.
rows.anchor: ولما تم بناؤها سار إليها بأهل مملكته فلما كان منها مسيرة يوم وليلة بعث الله تعالى عليهم صيحة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن قلابة
rows.claim: Ibn Qilabah's tale says he stumbled upon Iram while seeking camels, carried away what he could, and later recounted it to Muʿawiya.
rows.anchor: وعن عبد الله بن قلابة أنه خرج في طلب إبل له فوقع عليها فحمل ما قدر عليه

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb predicts that a short, reddish-blond Muslim with two moles will enter the city while Muʿawiya rules, then identifies Ibn Qilabah; al-Alusi calls this report fabricated too.
rows.anchor: فقال هي إرم ذات العماد وسيدخلها رجل من المسلمين في زمانك أحمر أشقر قصير

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid derives Iram from the verbal noun for perishing, making it mean destruction; he construes the wording as a simile and the relative clause as describing the city.
rows.anchor: وروي عن مجاهد أن إرم مصدر أرم يأرم إذا هلك فارم بمعنى هلاك منصوب على نحو نصب المصدر التشبيهي

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads the phrase with Iram in an annexation to ʿĀd, allowing Iram to be their ancestor or a city belonging to them.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن يعاد رام بإضافة ماد إلى أرم فجاز أن يكون إرم جدا

rows.speaker: ابن الزبير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr also reads ʿĀd in an annexation to Iram, with Iram pronounced as the name of a city in one dialect.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن الزبير بعاد أرم بالإضافة أيضا إلا أن أرم بفتح الهمزة وكسر الراء

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak is reported to read Iram with a lightened form, with or without declension.
rows.anchor: وعن الضحاك أنه قرأ بعاد مصروفا وغير مصروف أرم بفتح الهمزة وسكون الراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading annexes Iram to “the pillars,” understood as the landmarks of the city, while the following relative clause most naturally modifies “pillars.”
rows.anchor: وقريء إرم بإضافة إرم إلى ذات فقيل الأرم عليه العلم والمعنى بعاد أعلام ذات العماد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reads the verb as “made [it] ruins,” with “the pillared city” as its object; Iram can explain the verb or identify the ruined people or city.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أنه قرأ أرم بالتشديد فعلا ماضيا ذات بالنصب على المفعول به

rows.speaker: ابن الزبير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr reads the verb in the active voice, with “its like” as the object; he also has a first-person plural reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن الزبير لم يخلق مبينا للفاعل وهو ضميره عز وجل مثلها بالنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thamud is a well-known tribe named for its ancestor, brother of Jadis, descended through ʿAbir, Iram, and Sam from Noah; they were Arab peoples living at al-Hijr between the Hijaz and Tabuk and worshipped idols.
rows.anchor: وثمود عطف على عاد وهي قبيلة مشهورة سميت باسم جدهم ثمود أخي جديس وهما عابر بن إرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name is indeclinable as a proper feminine name; Ibn Waththab declines it when it denotes the people, and it may be Arabic from “little water” or foreign, as al-Raghib relates.
rows.anchor: ومنع الصرف للعلمية والتأنيث وقرأ ابن وثاب بالتنوين صرفه باعتبار الحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They cut the rock” means cutting mountain rock and hollowing homes in it, as in 7:74; a report says Thamud first carved stone and built 1,700 stone cities, which al-Alusi doubts.
rows.anchor: الذين جابوا الصخر أي قطعوا صخر الجبال واتخذوا فيها بيوتا نحتوها من الصخر كقوله تعالى وتنحتون من الجبال بيوتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The valley is Wadi al-Qura; the reading with yāʾ and the preposition may attach to the verb or function as a circumstantial phrase.
rows.anchor: بالواد هو وادي القرى وقريء بالياء آخر الحروف والباء للظرفية والجار والمجرور متعلق بجابوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some construe the preposition as instrument or cause: they cut the rock with or because of their valley, making it a water-place; al-Alusi says this is less apparent.
rows.anchor: أي جابوا الصخر بواديهم أو بسببه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The primary sense of jābū is literally to cut through; a cited poetic line uses the verb of traversing a land, while al-Raghib derives “answer” from cutting a hollow through speech.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر ولا رأيت قلوصاقبلها حملت

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib derives “answer” from cutting through a hollow in the earth, then extends it to crossing any land and to the reply that completes a question.
rows.anchor: وقال الراغب الجواب قطع الجوبة وهي الغائط من الأرض ثم يستعمل في قطع كل أرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh is called “possessor of stakes” because of his many soldiers and their tents, whose pegs they drove at their camps.
rows.anchor: وصف بذلك لكثرة جنوده وخيامهم التي يضربون أوتادها في منازلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that he had victims stretched face-down with four stakes and tortured them by beating, burning, or other means.
rows.anchor: أو لأنه كان يدق للمعذب أربعة أوتاد ويشده بها مبطوحا على الأرض فيعذبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause may be a genitive adjective for the named peoples, or nominative or accusative as a clause of censure; on the latter parsing each tyrant is meant.
rows.anchor: الذين طغوا في البلاد إما مجرور على أنه صفة للمذكورين عاد ومن بعده أو منصوب أو مرفوع على الذم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their abundant corruption consisted of disbelief and other sins.
rows.anchor: فأكثروا فيها الفساد أي بالكفر وسائر المعاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sent a severe punishment upon each group immediately after its tyranny and corruption; the genitive in “whip of punishment” can mean “from,” and the punishment is what befell them in varied forms.
rows.anchor: أي أنزل سبحانه إنزالا شديدا على كل طائفة من أولئك الطوائف عقيب ما فعلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sawṭ originally means mixing; it came to denote a braided whip, either because its strands are mixed or because it mixes flesh with blood.
rows.anchor: والسوط في الأصل مصدر من ساط يسوط إذا حلط قال الشاعر أحارث أنا لو تياط دماؤنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image of pouring signals abundance, succession, and continuity; the descent is compared to something liquid or flowing poured out forcefully.
rows.anchor: والتعبير عن إنزاله بالصب للإيذان بكثرته وتتابعه واستمراره فإنه عبارة عن إراقة شيء مائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say “whip” minimizes what befell them relative to the afterlife; al-Alusi notes that relative smallness can coexist with the image of abundant pouring.
rows.anchor: أفي الكشف أن إضافة السوط إلى العذاب تقليل لما أصابهم منه ولا يأبى ذلك التعبير بالصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis takes “punishment” as the act of punishing and the annexation as possession, or understands a mixed punishment like mixed strands of a whip.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يراد بالعذاب التعذيب والإضافة حينئذ على معنى اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other grammatical analyses treat sawṭ as a simile for kinds of punishment or as a passive verbal noun meaning a mixed punishment; al-Sihah also glosses it as a share or severity of punishment.
rows.anchor: وأن يكون السوط مصدرا بمعنى المفعول والإضافة كالأضافة في جرد قطيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers the earlier explanation as most fitting the eloquence of the revelation; the image resembles 16:112, where God makes people taste the garment of hunger.
rows.anchor: وأراد أن الغرض التصوير والأليق بجزالة التنزيل ما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This clause explains the punishment and warns that the Prophet's deniers will suffer what befell their predecessors; the Lord's designation emphasizes the relationship to him.
rows.anchor: تعليل لما قبله وإيذان بأن كفار قومه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم سيصيبهم مثل ما أصاب أضرابهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mirsād is the place where watchers wait, a pattern derived from the verb “watch” like mīqāt from “appoint.”
rows.anchor: والمرصاد المكان الذي يقوم به الرصد ويترقبون فيه مفعال من رصده

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak explains the metaphor as God keeping watch over the deeds of sinners and recompensing even the smallest act, with no escape.
rows.anchor: حافظا لأعمال العصاة على ما روي عن الضحاك مترقبا لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage figuratively compares God's preservation and recompense of deeds to a watcher waiting by a road to seize passersby; on this view it warns sinners generally.
rows.anchor: شبه كونه تعالى حافظا لأعمال العصاة على ما روي عن الضحاك مترقبا لها ومجازيا على نقيرها وقطميرها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: One view limits the warning to unbelievers; al-Hasan's apparent view makes it a threat to sinners and a promise to others.
rows.anchor: وقيل هي وعيد للكفرة وقيل وعيد للعصاة ووعد لغيرهم وهو ظاهر قول الحسن

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya proposes that al-mirsād is an intensive form, like words for a great eater or attacker; Abu Hayyan objects that the preposition bāʾ does not fit that usage.
rows.anchor: وجوز ابن عطية كون المرصاد صيغة مبالغة كالمطعام والمطعان وتعقبه أبو حيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reply makes the bāʾ an intensive rhetorical extension, but the analysis would entail applying “al-mirsād” as a name to God, which al-Alusi finds problematic.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بأنها على ذلك تجريدية نعم يلزمه إطلاق المرصاد على الله عز وجل وفيه شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage continues the warning: God watches for the afterlife, while people care only for worldly pleasure, becoming content when they get it and resentful when they do not.
rows.anchor: كأنه قيل أنه سبحانه لبالمرصاد من أجل الآخرة فلا يطلب عز وجل إلا السعي لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative makes the sentence follow as a consequence: the rich person becomes arrogant and the poor person despairs and says what should not be said; al-Alusi dismisses this reading.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو متصل به متفرع عليه على معنى فالإنسان يؤاخذ لا محالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God treats abundance as a test of gratitude; the fa in “honored him and gave him ease” explains what the test consists of, and the two actions are expressed as one in the person's reply.
rows.anchor: بتلاه ربه أي عامله معاملة من يبتليه بالغنى واليسار ليرى هل يشكر أم لا والفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause “my Lord honored me” is the predicate about the person; because “when” is delayed, it modifies “he says,” and the fa does not prevent this syntax.
rows.anchor: وهذه الجملة خبر للمبتدأ الذي هو الإنسان والفاء لما في أما من معنى الشرط والظرف أعني إذا متعلق بيقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, al-Safaqisi, and many commentators allow “when” to modify “he says” despite its post-fa position; al-Shihab calls this correct.
rows.anchor: كما صرح به الزمخشري وغيره من متقدمي النحاة وتبعهم من بعدهم كأبي حيان والسمين

rows.speaker: الرضي
rows.claim: Al-Radi and those following him, including al-Damamini, allow post-fa advancement only when the advanced phrase is the sole separator after “as for”; a second separator is disallowed.
rows.anchor: وخالفهم في ذلك الرضي ومن تبعه كالبدر الدماميني في شرح المغنى فقالوا

rows.speaker: الجلبي
rows.claim: Al-Jalabi claims this restriction is agreed and rejects the earlier parsing, proposing instead an omitted predicate such as “as for the person's state when …”.
rows.anchor: وزعم الجلبي محشي المطول إن هذا متفق عليه فرد به على المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi objects that the proposed “state” would make “he says” its predicate only through strained interpretation, so that rescue is not sound.
rows.anchor: ويرد على تقديره أنه لآ يصح وقوع جملة يقول خبرا عن الشأن إلا بتعسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding grammatical rescue avoids one difficulty only by fleeing from cloud to gutter, a proverb-like criticism; Abu al-Baqa instead makes “when” conditional and “he says” its answer, requiring an omitted clause.
rows.anchor: وهو فرار من السحاب إلى الميزاب وذهب أبو البقاء إلى أن إذا شرطية وقوله تعالى فيقول جوابها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poverty is likewise a test, here of patience; an implied “as for him” restores the balance with the preceding clause.
rows.anchor: وأما إذا ما ابتلآه عامله معاملة من يبتليه ويختبره بالحاجة والفقير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both replies are censured: restricted provision does not mean humiliation, and abundant provision is not a deserved honor based on lineage or status; God may grant honor in the afterlife through poverty.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن كلتا الجملتين متضمنة لأنكار قفول الإنسان الذي تضمنته وإنكار قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God calls the giving of wealth an honor only in the sense of granting it; the person wrongly claims that God gave it because he deserved special honor.
rows.anchor: وإنكار قوله إذا أكرم ربي أكرمني مع قوله تعالى فأكرمه أولا من حيث أنه إكرام الله تعالى له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative says only the claim of humiliation is denied: the person acknowledges God's generosity when given good, but wrongly calls its absence disgrace; al-Alusi prefers the earlier reading.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون الإنكار للإهانة فقط يعني أنه إذا تفضل عليه بالخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrasing recalls 70:19–21, where the human is anxious, despairing at harm, and withholding when good comes.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية مع ما بعد شمة من أسلوب قوله تعالى أن الإنسان خلق هلوعا إذا مسه الشر جزوعا

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir retains the final yāʾ in both first-person verbs; Nafi retains it in connected reading and drops it at pause, while Abu ʿAmr allows either.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير أكرمني وأهانني بإثبات الياء فيهما ونافع بإثباتها وصلا وحذفها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other five canonical readers drop the yāʾ in both forms in connected and paused reading; Abu Jaʿfar, ʿIsa, Khalid, al-Hasan in one report, and Ibn ʿAmir intensify the dāl in “qaddara.”
rows.anchor: وحذفها باقي السبعة فيهما وصلا ووقفا من حذفها وقفا سكن النون فيه وقرأ أبو جعفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “No” rebukes and denies both of the person's claims, not merely the second; al-Hasan explicitly supports this reading.
rows.anchor: كلا ردع للإنسان عن قوليه المحكيين وتكذيب له فيهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says neither wealth was given to honor the person nor poverty imposed to disgrace him; both are solely decree and determination.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما المعنى لم أبتله بالغنى لكرامته علي ولم أبتله بالفقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address shifts from censuring bad speech to worse conduct; direct address intensifies the rebuke, with the plural referring to humanity as a class.
rows.anchor: وقوله سبحانه بل لا تكرمون اليتيم الخ انتقال وترق من ذمه بالقبيح من القول إلى الأقبح من الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rich fail to fulfill the duty created by their wealth: they do not treat orphans kindly and generously.
rows.anchor: حيث يكرمكم الله تعالى بكثرة المال فلا تؤدون ما يلزمكم فيه من إكرام اليتيم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A prophetic report says the most beloved houses to God are those containing an honored orphan; al-Alusi gives no grading.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث أحب البيوت إلى الله تعالى بيت فيه ينيم مكرم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Abu Rajaʾ, Qatada, al-Jahdari, and Abu ʿAmr read the verb in the third person: “they do not honor.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن ومجاهد وأبو رجاء وقتادة والجحدري وأبو عمرو لا يكرمون بياء الغيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form “taḥāḍḍūn” drops one of the two tāʾs; people fail to urge and encourage one another to feed the needy.
rows.anchor: ولا تحاضون بحذف إحدى التاءين من تتحاضون أي ولا يحض ويحث بعضكم بعضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Food of the needy” means feeding them, with ṭaʿām used as a verbal noun like ʿaṭāʾ for giving.
rows.anchor: على طعام المسكين أي على إطعامه فالطعام مصدر بمعنى الإطعام كالعطاء بمعنى الإعطاء

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers taking the word as actual food and supplying an omitted “giving”: urging one another to provide the needy's food.
rows.anchor: وزعم أبو حيان أن الأولى أن يراد به الشيء المطعوم ويكون الكلام على حذف مضاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The needy here includes the poor generally; readings vary in the vowel of the tāʾ and between second- and third-person forms.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالمسكين ما يعم الفقير وقرأ عبد الله وعلقمة وزيد بن علي

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abd Allah, ʿAlqama, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Ibn al-Mubarak, and al-Shirizi from al-Kisaʾi read with a ḍamma on the tāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأ عبد الله وعلقمة وزيد بن علي وعبد الله بن المبارك والشيرزي عن الكسائي

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu ʿAmr, al-Hasan, and others read the verb in the third person without an alif after ḥāʾ; the other seven read it in second-person address.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو ومن سمعت الحسن ومن معه ولا يحضون بياء الغيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb may take an omitted object such as oneself, one's family, or anyone; al-Alusi prefers an intransitive reading that generalizes the rebuke.
rows.anchor: وجوز وهو الأولى أن يكون منزلا منزلة اللازم للتعميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-turāth means inheritance; its form replaces the initial wāw of wāriṯ with tāʾ, as in other Arabic words.
rows.anchor: وتأكلون التراث أي الميراث وأصله وارث فأبدلت الواو تاء كما في تخمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Lammā” means abundant collection or the act of gathering; the cited lines of al-Nabigha and al-Hutayʾa attest its usage.
rows.anchor: أكلا لما أي ذا لم أو هو نفس اللم على المبالغة واللم الجمع ومنه قول النابغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke targets combining one's inheritance share with others' lawful shares and with what is unlawful or blameworthy.
rows.anchor: والمراد به هنا الجمع بين الحلال والحرام وما يحمد وما لا يحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says they denied inheritance to women and young children, taking their shares on the claim that only those who fight and defend the clan inherit; they knew Ishmael's law allowed them to inherit.
rows.anchor: ويروى أنهم كانوا لا يورثون النساء ولا صغار الأولاد فيأكلون نصيبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This answers the objection that the chapter is Meccan while inheritance rules came later: their knowledge could come from Ishmael's law, and al-Alusi rejects rational moral knowledge of this legal distinction.
rows.anchor: فاندفع ما قيل أن السورة مكية وآية المواريث مدنية ولا يعلم الحلو الحرمة إلا من الشرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says heirs knowingly combine a deceased person's lawful and unlawful accumulated wealth.
rows.anchor: وقيل يعني تأكلون ما جمعه الميت المورث من حلال وحرام عالمين بذلك

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari allows a criticism of heirs who obtain wealth without toil and squander it on lavish arrays of food, drink, and fruit; al-Alusi says this does not fit the context.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشاف يجوز أن يذم الوارث

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains “much” as abundant; al-Alusi cites a line by Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt using the word similarly.
rows.anchor: وتحبون المال حبا جما أي كثيرا كما قال ابن عباس وأنشد قول أمية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their attachment to wealth is excessive and accompanied by greedy avarice.
rows.anchor: والمراد أنكم تحبونه مع حرص وضره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “No” rebukes the preceding greed, and the new clause opens a threat to explain the rebuke.
rows.anchor: كلا ردع لهم عن ذلك وقوله تعالى إذا دكت الأرض دكا دكا إلى آخره استئناف

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil defines dakk as breaking a wall, mountain, or similar structure; its repetition signals complete coverage, not simple emphasis.
rows.anchor: والدك قال الخليل كسر الحائط والجبل ونحوهما وتكريره للدلالة على الاستيعاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this reading the earth is repeatedly shaken and broken until mountains, buildings, and palaces vanish into scattered dust.
rows.anchor: أي إذا دكت الأرض دكا متتابعا حتى انكسر وذهب كل ما على وجهها من جبال

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad instead defines dakk as lowering raised ground by flattening it; the earth is levelled repeatedly until smooth like a rock.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد الدك حط المرتفع بالبسط والتسوية وندك سنام البعير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Either way, the phrase is said to describe what happens to the earth at the second blast of the trumpet.
rows.anchor: وأيا ما كان فهو على ما قيل عبارة عما عرض للأرض عند النفخة الثانية

rows.speaker: منذر بن سعيد
rows.claim: Munḏir ibn Saʿid says “your Lord came” means that God manifested to creation then, without a movement from place to place.
rows.anchor: قال منذر بن سعيد معناه ظهر سبحانه للخلق هنالك وليس ذلك بمجيء نقلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another construes the wording with an omitted “decree,” while the preferred view makes it a representation of God's manifested signs, power, and sovereignty.
rows.anchor: وقيل الكلام على حذف المضاف للتهويل أي وجاء ربك وقضاؤه سبحانه واختار جمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image is like a king's personal arrival, which inspires awe beyond the presence of his entire army and court.
rows.anchor: مثلت حاله سبحانه في ذلك بحال الملك إذا حضر بنفسه ظهر لمحضوره من آثار الهيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The angel” means the angelic host collectively; they descend by heavens and stand in ranks according to their stations and ranks.
rows.anchor: والملك أي جنس الملك فيشتمل جمع ملائكة السماوات عليهم السلام صفاصفا أي مصطفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says angels of each heaven form a rank around the earth, making seven ranks; another scholar takes “the angel” as all angels everywhere and compares their ordering to rows in prayer.
rows.anchor: وروي أن ملائكة كل سماء تكون صفا حول الأرض فالصفوف سبعة على ما هو الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the pronouns refer to God, no one but God administers His punishment and binding; the construction is a metonymy that heightens the punishment, contrary to Ibn al-Hajib's objection.
rows.anchor: الهاء إما لله عز وجل أي لا يتولى عذاب الله تعالى ووثاقه سبحانه أحد سواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the pronouns refer to the described human, the jailers punish and bind no one as severely as him; al-Alusi calls this good and ultimately prefers it.
rows.anchor: وأما للإنسان الموصوف والأضافة إلى المفعول أي لا يعذب ولا يوثق أحد من الزبانية أحدا

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Several readers, including al-Kisaʾi and Yaʿqub, use passive verbs, making the pronouns refer to the human who is punished and shackled beyond others for disbelief.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن سيرين وابن أبي إسحاق وأبو حيوة وابن أبي عبلة وأبو بحرية وسلام والكسائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the passive reading, the accusative nouns may be verbal nouns equivalent to “punishment” and “binding”; alternatively, the sense is that no one bears another's punishment, as in 6:164.
rows.anchor: ونصب العذاب على المصدرية واقع موقع التعذيب أما لأنه بمعناه في الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threatened human is generally anyone bearing the described traits; al-Alusi rejects identifying him with Iblis because Satan is not a human being.
rows.anchor: ثم الظاهر أن المراد جنس المتصف بما ذكر وقيل المراد به أمية ابن خلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Identifications with Umayya ibn Khalaf or Ubayy ibn Khalaf are contrary to the apparent general sense, even if the verse is said to have been revealed about one of them.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد به أمية ابن خلف وقيل أبي بن خلف وهو خلاف الظاهر

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar and, in one report, Shayba read “his binding” with a kasra on the wāw.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر وشيبة بخلاف عنه وثاقه بكسر الواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This passage depicts the state of one at rest through God's remembrance and obedience, contrasted with the person settled in worldly life; God is understood to be speaking, directly or through an angel, likely after judgment.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى يا أيها النفس المطمئنة الخ حكاية لا حوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation makes the nafs the self: reason ascends through causes to the First Cause, and the soul becomes calm upon knowing and relying wholly on God.
rows.anchor: والنفس قيل بمعنى الذات ووصفت بالاطمئنان بذلك لأنها لترقي بقوتها العاقلة في معارج الأسباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another, which al-Alusi calls a good interpretation, is the believer certain of truth, whose heart has no doubt or disturbance; this links remembrance to the strength of certainty and 39:9.
rows.anchor: وقيل هي النفس المؤمنة المطمئنة إلى الحق الواصلة إلى ثلج اليقين وبرودته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view is the believer who feels no fear or grief at resurrection; Abu's reading “secure, at rest” supports it and contrasts with the earlier grieving person.
rows.anchor: وقيل هي الأمنة التي لا يستفزها خوف ولا حزن يوم القيامة أعني النفس المؤمنة

rows.speaker: أبو
rows.claim: Abu reads “O secure soul, at rest,” connecting the two descriptions.
rows.anchor: وأيد بقراءة أبي يا أيتها النفس الآمنة المطمئنة

rows.speaker: زيد
rows.claim: Zayd reads the vocative particle without its tāʾ; the grammarian in al-Badiʿ explains why the form stays masculine with a feminine addressee, an analysis al-Alusi dismisses as irrelevant.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد على يا أيها بغير تاء وذكر صاحب البديع أن أيا قد تذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Return to your Lord” can mean returning after judgment to the station of divine care and honor, where the blessed wait before each is called to account.
rows.anchor: إرجعي أي من حيث حوسبت إلى ربك أي إلى محل عنايته تعالى وموقف كرامته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it tells the soul to turn its heart away from anxious concern about its deeds and attend wholly to God; after its accepted reckoning, the words reassure it that the matter is finished.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون المعنى ارجعي بتخلية القلب عن الأعمال والألتفات إليها والأهتمام بأمرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling her “the tranquil soul” is a rhetorical prompt, like telling a famous brave person to act bravely when he hesitates; “to your Lord” adds tenderness.
rows.anchor: ونداؤها بعنوان الأطمئنان لتذكيرها بما يقتضي الرجوع نظير قولك لشجاع مشهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Pleased” may mean pleased with God's endless gifts, or specifically relieved by an easy accounting and accepted deeds; al-Alusi says the latter is weak.
rows.anchor: راضية أي بما يؤتينه من النعم التي لا تتناهى وقد يقال راضية بما نلتيه من خفة الحساب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A view takes the two states as pleased with God and accepted by Him, but al-Alusi questions its fit with the context.
rows.anchor: وفل قيل المراد راضية عن ربك مرضية عنده وزعم أنه الأظهر واعترض بأنه غير مناسب للسياق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both adjectives are circumstantial accusatives; the first is apparently prospective, though some take it as simultaneous, and the second advances to the greater divine approval of 9:72.
rows.anchor: والوصفان منصوبان على الحال والظاهر أن الحال الأولى مقدرة وقيل مقارنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The soul is told to join the company of God's righteous, sincere servants and become one of their ranks.
rows.anchor: في زمرة عبادي الصالحين المخلصين لي وانتظمي في سلكهم وكوني في جملتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to enter the garden is coordinated with the preceding one: joining God's servants is spiritual happiness, while the garden is bodily happiness; the first is placed first as superior.
rows.anchor: وكان الأمر بالدخول في جملة عباد الله تعالى الصالحين إشارة إلى السعادة الروحانية

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan explains the preposition with entering a nonliteral sphere and its omission with a genuine container such as the garden.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حيان لأن المدخول فيه إن كان غير ظرف حقيقي تعدى إليه في الأستعمال بفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view reads “return to your Lord” as returning to the promised destination, meaning Paradise and the company of the righteous if the address comes after judgment.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد ارجعي إلى موعد ربك واستظهر أن المراد بموعده تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To answer the objection that returning implies prior residence in Paradise, one says souls were potentially present in Adam while he was in the garden; a similar interpretation of 28:85 takes “return” as Paradise, but it depends on identifying Adam's garden with the final one.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بتحقق هذا المقتضى بناء على وجودها بالقوة في ظهر آدم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another construes “return to your Lord” as returning to His command, meaning a gracious treatment, an honored station, or a comparable state.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد ارجعي إلى أمر ربك واستظهر أن المراد بالأمر على ذلك التقدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view makes it a return to God's honor, understood generally, because the soul was in the intermediate realm or after resurrection or judgment.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد ارجعي إلى كرامة ربك ويراد جنس كرامته سبحانه والرجوع إليه باعتبار

rows.speaker: عكرمة والضحاك
rows.claim: Ikrima and al-Dahhak place the address at resurrection and understand the soul as the person, with God as Lord; some supply an omitted noun for the return to His station.
rows.anchor: وعن عكرمة والضحاك أن ذلك القول عند البعث فقيل النفس بمعنى الذات أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading makes “soul” the spirit and “Lord” its owner, the body: it returns to its earthly body and then enters among God's servants and His reward.
rows.anchor: وقيل للنفس بمعنى الروح والمراد بالرب الصاحب وفسر بالجسد وباقي الآية على حالة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن جبير
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr reads “among My servants” as “among the bodies of My servants,” with the plural understood generically.
rows.anchor: وجاء هذا في رواية عن ابن عباس وابن جبير ولا يضر الإفراد أولا والجمع ثانيا

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and a group say the address comes at death, supported by a report transmitted from Saʿid ibn Jubayr.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد وجماعة أن ذلك القول عند الموت وأيد بما أخرجه عبد بن حميد

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report says the verse was recited before the Prophet; Abu Bakr praised it, and the Prophet said an angel would address him with it at death. Al-Alusi also cites a similar version in al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi.
rows.anchor: قال قرئت عند النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم يا أيتها النفس المطمئنة الآية فقال أبو بكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the death-time interpretation, “soul” means spirit: it returns at death to God's holy realm, enters the company of the near servants and the garden prepared for tranquil souls.
rows.anchor: والنفس عليه بمعنى الروح والمعنى على ما قيل ارجعي بالموت إلى عالم قدس ربك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this view the first entry follows death without delay, while entry into the garden of lasting residence follows at resurrection; because it is certain, both commands can nevertheless use immediate sequencing.
rows.anchor: وهذان الدخولان يعقبان الرجوع إلا أن الدخول الأول يعقبه بلا تراخ قبل يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other timings allow both entries immediately if the soul joins a righteous company and enjoys Paradise temporarily before resurrection; reports describe believers' spirits in birds in Paradise and a share of Paradise after death.
rows.anchor: ففي الحديث أن أرواح المؤمنين في حواصل طيور في الجنة وفي بعض الآثار إذا مات المؤمن أعطى نصف الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image of souls like polished mirrors reflecting one another's lights and increasing knowledge is dismissed by al-Alusi as rhetorical speculation.
rows.anchor: وذكر في وجه إدخالها مع الأرواح القدسية كالمرايا المصقولة فإذا انضم بعضها إلى بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Salih says “return to your Lord” refers to death and leaving the world, while entry among God's servants and into His garden occurs at resurrection.
rows.anchor: قال في الآية ارجعي إلى ربك هذا عنوا الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation places the address after death but before resurrection and takes “return” as return to the body for questioning by the two angels.
rows.anchor: وقيل أن هذا القول بعد الموت وقبل القيامة والمراد برجوعها إلى ربها رجوعها إلى جسدها

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb says the believer is shown his future home in Paradise at death, then told to return to the body, pleased with the reward shown, until Munkar and Nakir question him.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن المنذر عن محمد بن كعب القرظي أنه قال في الآية أن المؤمن إذا مات أرى منزله

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam says the believer is given the good news of Paradise at death, at resurrection, and on the day of gathering.
rows.anchor: وقيل أنه في مواطن ثلاثة أخرج ابن المنذر وابن أبي حاتم عن زيد بن أسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading that applies these commands to every time in worldly life makes them calls to continual obedience and good works, but al-Alusi says it should not count as a valid interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقيل يجوز أن يكون ذلك في سائر أوقات النفس في حياتها الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the address appears general across the proposed occasions rather than restricted to a single one.
rows.anchor: وأيا ما كان من الأوجه فالظاهر العموم فيها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report says the verse was revealed about ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan after he bought the well of Rumah and made it a public watering place; other proposed occasions name Hamza or Khubayb.
rows.anchor: وإن أخرج ابن أبي حاتم من طريق جويبر عن الضحاك عن ابن عباس أنها نزلت في عثمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The named Companions, including ʿUthman, Hamza, and Khubayb, are examples rather than exclusive referents; the occasion's form necessarily falls within the verse.
rows.anchor: فتفسير النفس المذكورة بأحد هؤلاء المذكورين كما نقل عن بعض من باب التمثيل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report through Ibn Mardawayh identifies the tranquil soul as the Prophet; al-Alusi likewise treats this as an illustrative application.
rows.anchor: وينبغي أن يتحمل قول ابن عباس في تلك النفس كما أخرجه عنه ابن مردويه هو النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some readings suggest that souls existed before bodies in the realm of the unseen; this issue is famous, while most theologians and Plato's school say souls are created when bodies are ready.
rows.anchor: وأشعرت الآية على بعض أوجهها بأن الأرواح مخلوقة قبل الأبدان ومقرها إذ ذاك في عالم الملكوت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, ʿIkrima, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, Abu Jaʿfar, Abu Salih, and the Yamani read “among My servant” in the singular, understood generically.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس وعكرمة والضحاك ومجاهد وأبو جعفر وأبو صالح وأبو شيخ اليماني في عبدي

rows.speaker: السادة الصوفية
rows.claim: Sufi teachers describe three ranks of the soul in this verse: tranquil, pleased, and approved; al-Alusi leaves their detailed exposition to their books.
rows.anchor: وللسادة الصوفية قدست نفوسهم كلام طويل في تقسيم مراتب النفس وقالوا أن الآية متضمنة لمراتب ثلاث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi quotes a supplication taught by the Prophet asking God for a tranquil soul that believes in meeting Him, accepts His decree, and is content with His gift.
rows.anchor: وأنا أقول كما علم رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم بعض الصحابة على ما أخرج الطبراني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next surah is Meccan according to most, though complete Medinan and mixed datings are also proposed; the reference to this city weighs against the latter, and al-Zamakhshari claims consensus on its Meccan origin.
rows.anchor: مكية في قول الجمهور بتمامها وقيل مدنية بتمامها وقيل مدنية إلا أربع آيات من أولها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some reports suggest the opening of the next surah was revealed in Mecca after the conquest.
rows.anchor: وسيأتي إن شاء الله تعالى أن في بعض الخبار ما هو ظاهر في نزول صدرها بمكة بعد الفتح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The transition links the surahs: after condemnation of hoarding wealth and neglecting the needy, the next passage names freeing slaves and feeding in famine; the tranquil soul is likewise linked to the path to contentment.
rows.anchor: ولما ذم سبحانه فيما قبلها من أحب المال وأكل التراث أكلا لما ولم يحض على طعام المسكين ذكر جل وعلا فيها الخصال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath is by the sacred city, which by agreement means Mecca; the surrounding oath concerns humanity's creation amid hardship and distress.
rows.anchor: أقسم سبحانه بالبلد الحرام أعني مكة فإنه المراد بالمشار إليه بالإجماع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following al-Kashshaf, al-Alusi takes the clause as an insertion between oath and its answer: the Prophet's hardship in the city also reproaches the polytheists for treating its most honored resident as violable.
rows.anchor: على ما اختاره في الكشاف اعترض بين القسم وجوابه وفيه تحقيق مضمونه بذكر بعض المكابدة

rows.speaker: شرحبيل بن سعد
rows.claim: Sharhabil ibn Saʿd says the polytheists forbid killing game and cutting trees in the sanctuary but deem expelling and killing the Prophet lawful there.
rows.anchor: عن شرحبيل بن سعد يحرمون أن يقتلوا به صيدا ويعضدوا شجره ويستحلون إخراجك وقتلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath strengthens the claim that hardship is inevitable, consoles the Prophet, and urges him to endure it; the city's honor also honors its resident.
rows.anchor: وفي تأكيد كون الإنسان في كيد بالقسم تثبيت لرسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes ḥill as “permitted”: Ibn Abbas says Muhammad may fight in Mecca while others may not.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس فيما أخرجه عنه ابن جرير وغيره وأنت يا محمد يحل لك أن تقاتل به

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says God made Mecca lawful for the Prophet for one hour; related reports say he was told to do what he wished on the day of conquest.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد أجله الله تعالى له عليه الصلاة والسلام ساعة من نهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Similar accounts are attributed to Abu Salih, Qatada, ʿAtiyya, Ibn Zayd, al-Hasan, and al-Dahhak, with the permission limited to the conquest.
rows.anchor: وروي نحو ذلك عن أبي صالح وقتادة وعطية وابن زيد والحسن والضحاك

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A prophetic report says Mecca was sacred from creation and would remain so, with only an hour's exception for the Prophet; it forbids cutting plants or frightening game, then permits the plant idhkhir at al-ʿAbbas's request.
rows.anchor: ثم قال عليه الصلاة والسلام إن الله تعالى حرم مكة يوم خلق السماوات والأرض فهي حرام إلى أن تقوم الساعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit “you” can imply exclusivity on Ibn Abbas's reading; ḥill is future-oriented if the surah predates the conquest, though a report from Ibn Jubayr suggests revelation after it if authentic, while most hold the earlier date.
rows.anchor: وتقديم المسند إليه على هذا للأختصاص كما أشير إليه في خبر ابن عباس وحل على معنى الستقبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view takes ḥill to mean that the Prophet is free of the inhabitants' sins; the insertion then honors his residence in the city while exposing the residents' diseased hearts.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون الحل على نحو ما ذكر في هذا الوجه لكن المعنى وأنت حل بهذا البلد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take the word as “dwelling” or “being present”; al-Alusi distinguishes its verbal and adjectival forms and rejects objections based on insufficient grammatical research.
rows.anchor: وقيل الحل صفة أو مصدر بمعنى الحال يقال حل أي نزل يحل حلا وحلولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause may be circumstantial; it magnifies Mecca by making the Prophet's presence there the basis of the oath's honor, and the demonstrative plus explicit noun add emphasis.
rows.anchor: وأيا ما كان ففي الإشارة وإقامة الظاهر مقام الضمير من تعظيم البلد ما فيهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A sound report from Ibn Abbas through Mujahid, also related from Mujahid, Qatada, and Saʿid ibn Jubayr, identifies the father as Adam and his offspring as all his descendants.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالأول آدم عليه السلام وبالثاني جميع ولده على ما أخرج الحاكم وصححه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other opinions take the pair as Adam and his righteous descendants, or Noah and his descendants.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد آدم عليه السلام والصالحون من ذريته وقيل نوح عليه السلام وذريته

rows.speaker: أبو عمران
rows.claim: Abu ʿImran says the pair is Abraham and all his children.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن جرير وابن أبي حاتم عن أبي عمران أنهما إبراهيم عليه السلام وجميع ولده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view specifies Abraham, Ishmael, and Muhammad because Abraham sanctified Mecca, Ishmael originated there, and Muhammad was born there; al-Alusi says the context may suggest this.
rows.anchor: وقيل إبراهيم عليه السلام وولده إسماعيل عليه السلام والنبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم ادعى أنه ينبيء عن ذلك

rows.speaker: الطبري والماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Tabari and al-Mawardi suggest that “father” is Muhammad because he was just mentioned, and “what he begot” is his community, supported by his saying he is like a father to them; al-Alusi dismisses this.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري والماوردي يحتمل أن يكون الوالد النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم لتقدم ذكره

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Another report attributed to Ibn Abbas through ʿIkrima says “father” is whoever begets and “what he begot” includes the infertile among men and women; the reading requires an omitted relative and conflicts with Basran grammar and the apparent sense.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي حاتم وغيره من طريق عكرمة عنه أنه قال الوالد الذي يلد وما ولد العاقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording likely leaves both terms unrestricted while invoking figures especially associated with Mecca, most likely Abraham and Ishmael; the indefinite form dignifies the father and mā magnifies the child.
rows.anchor: ولعل ظاهر اللفظ عدم التعيين في المعطوفين وظاهر العطف على هذاالبلد إرادة من له دخل فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using mā rather than man heightens wonder at the child, as in 3:36; humanity's reason, form, and other capacities also make the human being astonishing.
rows.anchor: وإيثار ما على من بناء على أن المراد بما ولد العاقل لأرادة الوصف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers to the person indicated by the context, who makes the Prophet endure hardship and violates the sanctuary; the threat applies to whoever deserves it.
rows.anchor: والضمير في قوله تعالى أيحسب على ما عدا ذلك راجع إلى ما دل عليه السياق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Possible specific occasions include Abu al-Ashadd Usayd ibn Kilda, who boasted that no one could defeat his strength; other candidates are ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Wudd, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Jahl, and al-Harith ibn ʿAmir.
rows.anchor: وقيل على إرادة البعض هو أبو الأشد أسيد بن كلدة الجحمي وكان شديد القوة مغترا بقوته

rows.speaker: عصام الدين
rows.claim: ʿIsam al-Din reads the question as astonishment at a person who thinks nobody can overpower or punish him despite his inability to escape hardship; it also implies disbelief in resurrection.
rows.anchor: وجعل عصام الدين الاستفهام للتعجيب على معنى أيظن أن لن يقدر عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lubadan means a great quantity, from the idea of things gathered together; the man says this boastfully to flaunt his spending over believers.
rows.anchor: يقول أهلكت مالا لبدا أي كثيرا من تلبد الشيء إذا اجتمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling his outlay “wasting” displays his indifference, as though the large amount had been thrown away without concern; one view says he spent it to oppose the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وعبر عن الأنفاق بالإهلاك إظهارا لعدم الأكتراث

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Mujahid? A report from Muqatil says al-Harith ibn Nawfal complained that he had spent great wealth on expiations and penalties since obeying Muhammad, after asking the Prophet how to expiate sins.
rows.anchor: فعن مقاتل أن الحرث بن نوفل كان إذا أذنب استقتى الرسول صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view has the speaker make this boast on Judgment Day, when his expenditure proves useless and is therefore called waste.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد ما تقدم أولا إلا أن هذا القول وقت الأنتقام منه وذلك يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar reads lubadan with a doubled b; he and Zayd ibn ʿAli also have a form with a still b, while Mujahid and Ibn Abi al-Zinad read both vowels as ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر لبدا بشد الباء وعنه وعن زيد بن علي لبدا بسكون الباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He may think nobody saw his spending, whether he sought public notice or spent in hostility to the Prophet; God observed it and will question and repay him.
rows.anchor: أي حين كان ينفق ما ينفق رئاه الناس أو حرصا على معاداته صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A prophetic report says a servant's feet will not move on Judgment Day until questioned about life, wealth and how it was earned and spent, and knowledge and its practice.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث لا تزول قدما العبد يوم القيامة حتى يسأل عن أربع عن عمره فيم أفناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading takes “see” as “find” and the past-form negation as certain future: God will find and reckon with him on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون المعنى إن لم يجده أحد على أن المراد بالرؤية الوجدان اللازم له

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the boastful speaker lied and spent nothing; God saw what he did or did not do and can expose and recompense him.
rows.anchor: وعن الكلبي أن هذا القائل كان كاذبا لم ينفق شيئا فقال تعالى أيظن أن الله تعالى ما رأى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave him two eyes with which to see.
rows.anchor: ألم نجعل له عينين يبصر بهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tongue expresses what is within, and the lips cover the mouth and assist speech, eating, drinking, blowing, and other acts.
rows.anchor: ره وشفتين يستر بهما فاه ويستعين بهما على النطق والأكل والشرب والنفخ وغير ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular “lip” is shafah, originally shafhah with its hāʾ dropped; despite its feminine tāʾ, it does not take the regular alif-tāʾ plural, according to al-Bahr.
rows.anchor: والمفرد شفة وأصلها شفهة حذفت منها الهاء وبدل عليه شفيهة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: The established interpretation is the two ways of good and evil, reported from Ibn Masʿud with al-Hakim's authentication, from Ibn Abbas, and from ʿIkrima, al-Dahhak, and others; Abu Umama transmits it from the Prophet.
rows.anchor: أي طريقي الخير والشر كما أخرجه الحاكم وصححه والطبراني وغيرهما عن ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Najd is a raised road; al-Alusi cites a line by Imruʾ al-Qays about crossing Najd and explains the region's height relative to Tihama.
rows.anchor: والنجد مشهور في الطريق المرتفع قال امرؤ القيس فريقان منهم جازع بطن نخلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessing lies in making clear which route saves and which ruins; the blessing does not depend on the person choosing the good route.
rows.anchor: والأمتنان المحدث عنه بأن هداه سبحانه وبين له تعالى شأنه ما أن سلكه نجا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Imam links this to 76:3: God showed the human the way, whether grateful or ungrateful.
rows.anchor: وقد جعل الإمام هذه الآية كقوله تعالى إنا هديناه السبيل إما شاكرا وإما كفورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the good path elevated is apt; evil is a descent from innate human nature to misery, either by contrast or by imagining the climb toward it.
rows.anchor: ووصف سبيل الخير بالرفعة والنجدة ظاهر بخلاف سبيل الشرفان فيه هبوطا من ذروة الفطرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: An alternative from Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Musayyib identifies the two heights as the mother's breasts: paired routes providing an infant life and nourishment.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن جرير وابن أبي حاتم من طرق عن ابن عباس أنهما الثديان روي ذلك عن ابن المسيب

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report says Ali rebuked people who claimed the heights meant breasts and clarified that they are good and evil; al-Alusi allows that the alternative relies on the wording and obvious benefaction.
rows.anchor: ونسب هذا التفسير لعلي كرم الله تعالى وجهه أيضا والمذكور في الدر المنثور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iqtihām is entering forcefully and quickly, while an ʿaqaba is a steep, difficult mountain path; here it metaphorically names arduous deeds of high rank before God.
rows.anchor: الأقتحام الدخول بسرعة وضغط وشده ويقال قحم في الأمر قحوما رمى نفسه فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imagery may instead make performing those deeds itself a hard ascent; following the two paths makes the metaphor especially eloquent.
rows.anchor: والقرينة ظاهرة وإثبات المراد به الفعل والكسب ترشيح ويجوز أن يكون قد جعل فعل ما ذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse censures the person for failing to thank God for immense gifts through righteous deeds, instead denying the blessing and following desire.
rows.anchor: والمراد ذم المحدث عنه بأنه مقصر مع ما أنعم الله تعالى به عليه من النعم العظام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maqraba is a verbal noun for kinship, so “orphan of kinship” means a related orphan; al-Zajjaj calls “he is my kinship” poor usage and a cited couplet contrasts stranger and relative.
rows.anchor: يتيما ذا مقربة أي قرابة فهو مصدر ميمي أيضا من قرب في النسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Feeding such an orphan combines almsgiving with maintaining family ties, multiplying the reward; another view includes someone close by neighborly relation.
rows.anchor: وفي إطعام هذا جمع بين الصدقة والصلة وفيهما من الأجر ما فيهما وقيل أنه لا يخص القريب نسبا
